title: Search systems and inverted indexes
subtitle: A search engine does not scan your text. It looks words up in an inverted index, ranks the matches, and must be kept in step with your database.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is common. A small shop has a search box. The code runs
SELECT * FROM products WHERE title ILIKE '%shoe%'
Two years later there are 3 million products. Each search now reads every row, because no normal index can help with a pattern that starts with
. During a sale, searches use most of the database CPU, and checkout slows down too.
The results are also poor. A search for "running shoes" does not find "Shoe for runners". The results come back in no useful order.

So the team adds Elasticsearch. The code saves each product to Postgres and then to Elasticsearch. One night the Elasticsearch call times out for some saves. The prices in search no longer match the real prices, and nobody notices for a week.
Both problems have known fixes. This lesson explains them.
The Postgres docs list three problems with
search. It has no language support, so
. It does not rank results. And it tends to be slow, because there is no index support, so it must process every document for every search.
A search engine fixes this in two steps.
, it splits the text into words, cleans each word, and records which documents contain it.
, it cleans the query words the same way, looks them up, and ranks the matching documents.
The record from step 1 is an
. A book index is a good picture: "replication, pages 40, 112, 305". You do not read the whole book to find a word.
Search is fast because the work happens when you write. Each document is broken into terms once, and each term points to its documents. A query reads only a few short lists.
Step through three product titles, the index built from them, and one query. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
breaks text into small pieces called tokens. Normalization makes near matches equal. It can lowercase
Postgres does the same work with dictionaries. Its normalized words are called
Elasticsearch can apply the same rules to the query text.
Always do this. If the index holds
Lucene's docs call the inverted index its core. It is made of
, which let you look up the documents for a given term.
It can also store the positions of a term inside each document.
Positions make phrase search possible, like "red shoes" as two words side by side.
Postgres has an inverted index too. Its GIN index has one entry for each lexeme, with a compressed list of where it appears. The docs call GIN the preferred index type for text search.
A query for "red shoes" may match 40,000 products. Which come first? The engine gives each match a score.
. Lucene's docs explain its parts. A document that contains a term more often scores higher. Rarer terms add more to the score. And a match in a shorter field counts for more.
So "jacket" in 10 products tells you more than "red" in 50,000 products.

It is the default similarity in Elasticsearch.

You rarely change these. Most relevance work is in the analyzer, the fields you search and the boosts you add.

New documents are not searchable the moment you write them. Elasticsearch collects them and, on a refresh, writes them to a new segment and opens it for search. A segment is similar to an inverted index.
By default, Elasticsearch refreshes every second. It only does this for indices that got at least one search request in the last 30 seconds.
You can ask a write to wait.
makes the change visible at once, but it creates tiny segments that cost more at index, search and merge time.
waits for the next refresh instead. The docs say to use the default,
, unless you have a good reason.
An Elasticsearch index is split into shards. Each shard is a self-contained Lucene index with part of the documents. Each document belongs to one primary shard. A
shard is a copy of a primary, for
You choose the number of primary shards when you create the index, and you cannot change it later. You can change the number of replicas at any time.
Each shard runs a search on one CPU
. Too many small shards slow search and can make the cluster unstable. Elastic suggests shards between 10 GB and 50 GB.

The search index is a copy. Your database is the source of truth. The dangerous design is the one from the story: write to the database, then write to the search engine in the same request. If the second write fails, the copy is wrong, and nothing repairs it.
Safer designs read changes from the database itself:
as the product change, insert a row into an outbox table. A worker reads it and updates the index.
A tool reads the database's change log and sends each change to the indexer.

is harmless. Keep a script that rebuilds the whole index from the database, because you will need it after mapping changes.
You may not need a second system. Postgres gives you
of each matching document, so it can be slow when a query matches many rows.

Start with Postgres when the data fits in one database and the search needs are simple. Move to a search engine when you need better relevance, typo tolerance, facets, or search load that would hurt your main database.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "How many rows will this read in a year?"
Write down the analyzer for each field. Test it with real queries from your users, including plurals, accents and typos.
Treat the search index as derived data. Ask in design review:
"How do we rebuild it from scratch, and how long does that take?"
Monitor sync lag: the time between a database change and when search shows it. Alert on it.
on every write to fix "I can't see my change". Use
only where a user must see their own write.
Pick shard counts from expected data size, not from a guess. The primary count is fixed, so changing it means building a new index.
Keep a small set of test queries with the results you expect. Run it after each analyzer or scoring change.
"Find every SQL query in this repo that uses LIKE or ILIKE with a leading %. For each, estimate the table size and suggest a full-text index or a search engine."
"Add a Postgres full-text search on products.title and products.description, with a GIN index on a generated tsvector column, and rank with ts_rank."
"Write an outbox worker that reads product changes and sends the full document to Elasticsearch by ID. It must be safe to run twice."
The query uses the same language config or analyzer as the index. Otherwise matches are missed.
The agent did not add a direct database-then-search write in the request path.
Index writes use the document ID, so retries replace instead of adding duplicates.
Test with real queries, not just the one the agent picked.

options.v: LIKE is only slow in MySQL.
A normal B-tree index cannot help with a leading %, so every row must be checked.
The database caches the wrong rows.

why.v: The Postgres docs say LIKE searches have no index support, so they must process all documents for every search.

q.v: What does an inverted index store?

options.v: For each document, the list of its words.
For each term, the list of documents that contain it.

why.v: An inverted index maps a term to its postings, the documents that contain the term.

q.v: In BM25 and TF-IDF scoring, which word adds the most to a document's score?

options.v: A rare word that appears in only a few documents.
The longest word in the query.

why.v: Inverse document frequency gives rare terms a bigger weight, because they say more about which documents match.

q.v: You save a product, then search for it at once, and it is not found. What is the most likely reason in Elasticsearch?

options.v: The index has not refreshed yet, so the new segment is not open for search.
Replicas do not hold new documents.

why.v: Search is near real-time. New documents become searchable after a refresh, by default within about a second for indices that are being searched.

q.v: Your service writes to Postgres and then to Elasticsearch. The second write sometimes fails. What is a safer design?

options.v: Retry the Elasticsearch write in the request until it works.
Write an outbox row in the same database transaction, or use CDC, and let a worker update the index.
Write to Elasticsearch first, then Postgres.

why.v: The database stays the source of truth. A worker reads changes from it and updates the index, so no change is lost.
